blocks.text: 2.4 Stakeholder insights
Collaboration and data sharing are the barriers stakeholders raise most often, and the supply-side constraints they rate most severe.
What was asked

The inception report committed the study to interviews, focus groups and roundtables with key stakeholders, with their insights carried into the final report (Inception Report, Nov 2025, p22). This work answers SLA Annexure B clauses 1.1.6 and 3.2.8. [Clause wording to be checked against the signed Annexure B.]
What was done

Engagement runs in four phases: introduction and framing from January to March 2026, sense-making and validation, strategy socialisation and mobilisation into October (Stakeholder Insights Report, Mar 2026, p4, p17). The March report closes the first phase. It holds insight tables for 16 organisations, from Mossel Bay to the CTICC, carrying 223 insights rated 115 High, 102 Medium and 6 Low (p20 to p46, counted).

The method had four steps: run the sessions, extract insights, map each to the hypothesis tree and aggregate (Stakeholder Insights Report, Mar 2026, p5). The insights are the project team's concise statements, not verbatim quotations. This report therefore attributes them to organisations and quotes them as insight statements.

The record has two gaps. No airline, online travel agent or tour operator sits in the first phase; six such engagements, among them Trip.com, Emirates and SATSA, were proposed for the second (Stakeholder Insights Report, Mar 2026, p16). The outcomes of phases two to four are in no document in hand. [Letsema to supply the phase 2 to 4 engagement record for Appendix A6.]
Findings that survived into the tree

**1. Collaboration and data are the most widely shared concerns.** Fifteen of the 16 organisations raised industry and government collaboration and fifteen raised policy and data sharing (Stakeholder Insights Report, Mar 2026, p20 to p46, counted). Data sharing also carries the most insights (30) and the most High ratings (16).

blocks.caption: Fifteen of 16 organisations raised collaboration and fifteen raised policy and data sharing, more than any other theme.
blocks.source: Stakeholder Insights Report, Mar 2026, p20 to p46: number of the 16 organisations with at least one insight under each hypothesis-tree element, counted from the appendix tables. The report prints no tally.

blocks.text: The organisations describe the data architecture as "too fragmented, lagged and proxy-based to provide a reliable view of visitor volumes, spend, spread or economic impact at provincial level" (Stakeholder Insights Report, Mar 2026, p13). Platforms for collaboration already exist: FEDHASA points to JAMS, through which tourism associations coordinate with Wesgro, the Western Cape Government and the City of Cape Town (p31).

**2. The province cannot yet measure what the strategy targets.** The national Department of Tourism reports that "there is no approved official methodology for provincial tourism GDP and jobs estimates", rated High (Stakeholder Insights Report, Mar 2026, p37). Stats SA cites 749 vacancies behind delays to the tourism satellite account and infers provincial flows partly from ports-of-entry data (p30).

**3. Supply constraints are rated the most severe.** Of the 68 insights under Transform Supply, 44 are rated High, against 23 of 64 under Reshape Demand (Stakeholder Insights Report, Mar 2026, p20 to p46, counted). Weak public transport, congestion and unreliable last-mile access are called "structural barriers to visitor movement within and beyond Cape Town" (p10). Peak queues at the Table Mountain Aerial Cableway run up to three hours up and two hours down (p36).

**4. Funding and institutions have weakened.** The Department of Economic Development rates destination funding "materially below peer destinations" and reports that tourism institutional capacity "has eroded over the past decade at both provincial and municipal level", both High (Stakeholder Insights Report, Mar 2026, p25). National Treasury's MFMA Circular No. 131 of 31 March 2025 has disrupted municipal funding for local tourism bodies, most of which "are not operationally sustainable without municipal funding support" (p25).

Mandates blur at district level. The West Coast District Municipality reports "a mandate disconnect" between district, local municipalities and local tourism organisations that leaves tourism development without a clear owner (Stakeholder Insights Report, Mar 2026, p39). Fiscal pressure is turning attention to a tourism levy and blended finance (p25, p23).

**5. The binding levers sit nationally.** The Department of Economic Development reports that "restrictive bilateral air agreements are limiting airlift growth", rated High, and that SA Tourism's institutional weakness constrains international marketing (Stakeholder Insights Report, Mar 2026, p24, p25). Four organisations raised visas, among them the Cableway for India and China and the CTICC for African events (p36, p45). Seven raised safety, which the report calls a barrier across transport, township tourism and international selling (p10).

**6. The flagship sites are at capacity and exposed to weather.** Boulders is "already near carrying capacity" and summit expansion on Table Mountain is severely limited (Stakeholder Insights Report, Mar 2026, p24, p36). Robben Island loses about R16 million a year to weather-cancelled trips, and CapeNature reports climate-related flooding, fire and heat closing sites (p33, p43).

**7. Much product cannot be booked online.** CapeNature takes about 70% of its reservations through its call centre rather than its online platform (Stakeholder Insights Report, Mar 2026, p42). The Department of Economic Development rates destination platforms behind international practice in online presence and AI adoption, and the Overberg says its proximity to Cape Town is not packaged before travellers book flights (p24, p26).

**8. Some constraints went unraised.** No stakeholder named Cape Town International's capacity as a constraint; the airport appears only as a transfer-time reference (Stakeholder Insights Report, Mar 2026, p22, p43). Cruise is raised only by Mossel Bay, where calls rose from four before COVID to 27 a season (p20). The demand-side and airport voices were scheduled for later phases, so their absence here is a gap in the record, not a finding.
The report closes on eight areas for deeper engagement, which frame the questions the later phases were to test (Stakeholder Insights Report, Mar 2026, p14).

blocks.title: What this means for the tree
paras: **Validates FA17, Strengthen industry and government collaboration, and FA18, Expedite tourism-enabling policy and data sharing.** Each raised by 15 of 16 organisations, with existing platforms such as JAMS to build on (findings 1 and 2).

**Rewords FA16, Align institutional stakeholders across all three tiers, and supports FA19, Lead removal of infrastructure, visa and safety deficits.** Air rights, visas and SA Tourism sit nationally; mandates blur at district level (findings 4 and 5).
**Rewords FA14, Manage climate risk and sustainable tourism, and supports FA15, Crowd in capital.** Unfunded local tourism bodies and climate losses at flagship sites (findings 4 and 6).
**Supports FA03, FA09, FA10 and FA12.** Product that cannot be booked online, last-mile access, a narrow product set and flagships at capacity (findings 3, 6 and 7).

**Supplies the case for FA20, Develop workforce and service skills, as a question.** Skills gaps raised by CapeNature, the West Coast and the Overberg, with no labour analysis behind them (p27, p39, p43).
